'''Bella Abramovna Subbotovskaya''' (17 December 1937 – 23 September 1982)<ref>{{cite web|last1=O'Connor|first1=J|last2=Robertson|first2=E|title=Bella Abramovna Subbotovskaya|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Subbotovskaya/|website=MacTutor History of Mathematics|publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews, Scotland|accessdate=9 April 2024}}</ref> was a Soviet mathematician who founded the short-lived [[Jewish People's University]] (1978–1983) in [[Moscow]].<ref name="nams_2007">[[George Szpiro|Szpiro, G.]] (2007), "[https://www.ams.org/notices/200710/tx071001326p.pdf Bella Abramovna Subbotovskaya and the Jewish People's University]", ''[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]'', '''54'''(10), 1326–1330.</ref><ref name="failed_2005">Zelevinsky, A. (2005), "Remembering Bella Abramovna", ''You Failed Your Math Test Comrade Einstein'' (M. Shifman, ed.), [[World Scientific]], 191–195.</ref> The school's purpose was to offer free education to those affected by structured anti-Semitism within the Soviet educational system. Its existence was outside Soviet authority and it was investigated by the [[KGB]]. Subbotovskaya herself was interrogated a number of times by the KGB and shortly thereafter was hit by a truck and died, in what has been speculated was an [[assassination]].<ref name="maa">{{Cite web|url=http://www.maa.org/news/math-news/remembering-math-heroine-bella-abramovna-subbotovskaya|title= Remembering Math Heroine Bella Abramovna Subbotovskaya|work=Math in the News|date=12 November 2007|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|accessdate=28 June 2014}}</ref>

== Academic work ==
Prior to founding the Jewish People's University, Subbotovskaya published papers in [[mathematical logic]]. Her results on Boolean formulas written in terms of <math>\land</math>, <math>\lor</math>, and <math>\lnot</math> were influential in the then nascent field of [[computational complexity theory]].

=== Random restrictions ===
Subbotovskaya invented the method of random restrictions to [[Boolean function]]s.<ref name="jukna">{{cite book|last1=Jukna|first1=Stasys|title=Boolean Function Complexity: Advances and Frontiers|date=Jan 6, 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3642245084|pages=167–173}}</ref> Starting with a function <math>f</math>, a restriction <math>\rho</math> of <math>f</math> is a partial assignment to <math>n-k</math> of the <math>n</math> variables, giving a function <math>f_\rho</math> of fewer variables. Take the following function:

:<math>f(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (x_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\lnot x_1 \lor x_2) \land (x_1 \lor \lnot x_3)</math>.

The following is a restriction of one variable

:<math>f_\rho(y_1, y_2) = f(1, y_1, y_2) = (1 \lor y_1 \lor y_2) \land (\lnot 1 \lor y_1) \land (1 \lor \lnot y_2)</math>.

Under the usual identities of [[Boolean algebra]] this simplifies to <math>f_\rho(y_1, y_2) = y_1</math>.

To sample a random restriction, retain <math>k</math> variables uniformly at random. For each remaining variable, assign it 0 or 1 with equal probability.

=== Formula Size and Restrictions ===

As demonstrated in the above example, applying a restriction to a function can massively reduce the size of its formula. Though <math>f</math> is written with 7 variables, by only restricting one variable, we found that <math>f_\rho</math> uses only 1.

Subbotovskaya proved something much stronger: if <math>\rho</math> is a random restriction of <math>n-k</math> variables, then the expected shrinkage between <math>f</math> and <math>f_\rho</math> is large, specifically

:<math>\mathbb{E} \left [ L(f_\rho) \right ] \le \left ( \frac k n \right )^{3/2} L(f)</math>,

where <math>L</math> is the minimum number of variables in the formula.<ref name="jukna" /> Applying [[Markov's inequality]] we see

:<math>\Pr \left [ L(f_\rho) \le 4 \left ( \frac k n \right )^{3/2} L(f) \right ] \ge \frac 3 4</math>.

=== Example application ===

Take <math>f</math> to be the [[parity function]] over <math>n</math> variables. After applying a random restriction of <math>n-1</math> variables, we know that <math>f_\rho</math> is either <math>x_i</math> or <math>\lnot x_i</math> depending the parity of the assignments to the remaining variables. Thus clearly the size of the circuit that computes <math>f_\rho</math> is exactly 1. Then applying the [[probabilistic method]], for sufficiently large <math>n</math>, we know there is some <math>\rho</math> for which

:<math>L(f_\rho) \le 4 \left ( \frac 1 {n} \right )^{3/2} L(f)</math>.

Plugging in <math>L(f_\rho) = 1</math>, we see that <math>L(f) \ge n^{3/2}/4</math>. Thus we have proven that the smallest circuit to compute the parity of <math>n</math> variables using only <math>\land, \lor, \lnot</math> must use at least this many variables.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kulikov|first1=Alexander|title=Circuit Complexity Minicourse: The Shrinkage Exponent of Formulas over U2|url=http://logic.pdmi.ras.ru/~kulikov/formulaminicourse/lecture4-slides.pdf|accessdate=22 January 2017}}</ref>

=== Influence ===

Although this is not an exceptionally strong lower bound, random restrictions have become an essential tool in complexity.
In a similar vein to this proof, the exponent <math>3/2</math> in the main lemma has been increased through careful analysis to <math>1.63</math> by [[Mike Paterson|Paterson]] and [[Uri Zwick|Zwick]] (1993) and then to <math>2</math> by [[Johan Håstad|Håstad]] (1998).<ref name="jukna" />
Additionally, Håstad's [[Switching lemma]] (1987) applied the same technique to the much richer model of constant depth [[Boolean circuits]].
